stories.primary_headline: Those opposing electoral roll revision attempting to undermine democracy: Suresh Gopi

primary_source.headline: Those opposing electoral roll revision attempting to undermine democracy: Suresh Gopi
primary_source.content: Mangaluru: Those opposing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls are attempting to undermine country’s democracy and electoral system, Union Minister of State for Petroleum and Natural Gas Suresh Gopi charged on Friday."Future generations will regard them as betrayers of trust and traitors to the nation," emphasised the actor Suresh Gopi. He was addressing gathering after inaugurating a public meeting organised as part of Bharatiya Janata Party’s ‘Save Democracy, End Anarchy campaign at Kadri ground. Suresh Gopi quoting a verse from renowned Tamil poet Subramania Bharathiyar's famous poem, ‘Bharata Samudayam Vazhgave; Vazhga Vazhga Bharata Samudayam Vazhgave’, declared that it was unfortunate that a ruling party had been compelled to organise a protest in response to an agitation organised by the opposition.He alleged that those spreading misinformation about the SIR, which is being undertaken to ensure the integrity of electoral politics, were misleading the country’s youth. Mangaluru: Union minister Suresh Gopi to take part in march against Congress over electoral rolls misinformation“Kharge’s son should understand that Narendra Modi is not going anywhere from this country. It is your leader and his family who should leave. If they do not go voluntarily, the people themselves will lift them up and throw them into the Arabian Sea,” Suresh Gopi declared.He added that the protest meeting was only the beginning and warned that the anger of the people would engulf all those opposing the initiative.BJP national spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia, BJP DK district president Satish Kumpala, Udupi district president Naveen Shetty Kuthyaru, Kasaragod district president N L Ashwini, MP Captain Brijesh Chowta, Kota Srinivas Poojary, MLAs D Vedavyas Kamath, Harish Poonja, Rajesh Naik Ulipadyguthu, K Umanath Kotian, Gurme Suresh Shetty, Bhagirathi Murulya, Gururaj Gantihole, Dr Y Bharath Shetty, Yashpal Suvarna, Kiran Kumar Kodgi, MLCs Kishore Kumar Puttur, Pratapsimha Nayak among olthers participated in the meeting.

stories.primary_headline: The Assassin review – will anybody save Keeley Hawes from this unbearably pathetic boy?

primary_source.headline: The Assassin review – will anybody save Keeley Hawes from this unbearably pathetic boy?
primary_source.content: The star is excellent in her return as a midlife assassin. But her whiny son is so annoying, the drama disintegrates into a soggy spy sitcom – he might just have killed the whole showSo there’s an assassin, right? Except, it’s not just AN assassin, it’s THE assassin. The world’s top assassin. Going round doing the most elite assassinations you can think of, being paid millions to kill super-dangerous people. Right? OK, But … it’s a woman – no, not like in Killing Eve. Well, OK, it is quite a lot like Killing Eve but wait: it’s not just a woman, it’s a sarcastic middle-aged British woman who hasn’t got time for anyone’s shit, And she’s got a difficult relationship with her adult son who doesn’t know she’s a killer! Boom!One day a few years ago, prolific TV thriller writers Harry and Jack Williams (since The Missing in 2014 they’ve created Rellik, The Widow, Liar, Baptiste, Angela Black, Boat Story and The Tourist) pitched something like the above in a meeting with Prime Video, and walked out of the room with a big bag of money and a commission for another of their slick, twisty dramas. With Keeley Hawes as sardonic mercenary Julie Green and Freddie Highmore as her wan, bookish journalist son Edward, the premise of The Assassin just about survived a chaotic first season that benefited from placing its two leads inside a labyrinthine conspiracy. Continue reading...

stories.primary_headline: ‘It’s a new world. It’s a little fascistic. And it needs a different response’: U2 on 50 years together – and why Bono can’t work with Trump

primary_source.headline: ‘It’s a new world. It’s a little fascistic. And it needs a different response’: U2 on 50 years together – and why Bono can’t work with Trump
primary_source.content: After some so-so albums, can U2’s new one, Carnaval de Luz, restore them to glory? They discuss male egos, working with Dolly Parton, and explain why, despite Trump, they still believe in democracy – at least in their bandLa Petite Maison, in Nice, has a certain reputation as a five-star celebrity haunt. Beyoncé eats here. So do Elton John, Tom Cruise, Harry Styles and Leonardo DiCaprio, their meals presided over by the restaurant’s founder, Nicole, variously described in print as “eccentric”, “unique” and “truculent” (she’s standing by the entrance when I arrive, and suffice to say, doesn’t look like someone you’d much enjoy being on the wrong side of).It’s enough of a celebrity haunt that the arrival of U2 – still incontrovertibly one of the biggest bands in the world 40 years after they could first reasonably have called themselves such – causes barely a murmur of interest among their fellow lunchtime diners. Then again, Bono is a regular. He was eating on the outdoor terrace the night of Nice’s terrorist attack, on Bastille Day in 2016, in which 86 people were killed. “I climbed through that window and hid under there,” he nods, pointing to a table at the rear of the restaurant. “Nicole,” he adds, “didn’t hide.” Continue reading...

primary_source.content: The country star has abandoned Nashville slickness for a set of raw, pared-back songs that reckon with the death of her mother and decades of personal struggles. ‘This is a labour of love,’ she saysWhen Wynonna Judd appears on my laptop screen – hair a deep shade of crimson, makeup perfect and sporting a huge black baseball cap with Kentucky Queen spelt out across its brim – she looks both fabulous and confident. Which is a good thing, as the Nashville star has been off the radar for a decade. On the occasions her name has made the news, it’s more often been linked to family tragedy than music.“I’m in a good place,” says the woman Rolling Stone described as “the greatest female country singer since Patsy Cline”. “My life has been chaotic. I’ve had a lot of success and a lot of failure, and it’s music that keeps me going. Always.” Continue reading...

stories.primary_headline: Rocky review – 50 years on, Stallone’s boxer remains an exhilaratingly gritty contender

primary_source.headline: Rocky review – 50 years on, Stallone’s boxer remains an exhilaratingly gritty contender
primary_source.content: The actor’s triumphant breakthrough has clear ancestors in grimy tales of working-class struggle, but finds a fresh, rousing idealismPeter Farrelly’s new film I Play Rocky is about the underdog-with-heart story of how a great boxing movie got made against the odds with its plucky young untried screenwriter allowed to star. So here is a reissue of that 1976 film for its 50th anniversary. It’s a forthright, rousingly idealistic film, wholesome in its essential patriotism, and which unselfconsciously shrugs off the boxing-movie’s gloomy generic inheritance, throwing away its grim traditional baggage of tragedy, cynicism and loss. It also doubles as a love letter to Philadelphia, the cradle of American democracy.Its writer and insurgent star Sylvester Stallone created the role of Rocky Balboa, a punchy heavyweight fighter just turned 30, making peanuts slugging it out with bums and reduced to collecting debts for the Philly mob; this is an indignity which infuriates his grizzled old trainer and former mentor Mickey (Burgess Meredith) who once saw greatness in Rocky and is disgusted to see him selling out. Rocky is moreover entirely oblivious to national preparations to celebrate the 1976 bicentennial. (Boxing is for this anniversary what country music was in Robert Altman’s Nashville, only without the disorientation and pessimism.) Continue reading...

primary_source.headline: Enrico Rava Fearless Five with Joe Lovano: Corners review | John Fordham's jazz album of the month
primary_source.content: (ECM)The Italian trumpeter’s group – featuring an old friend – rip through originals and free improvisation while balancing late-Miles funk with excellent vocals and horn balladsMiles Davis was the gamechanger behind at least three landmark transformations in jazz-making methods between the late 1940s and the 1960s – yet he was perhaps too instinctively lyrical, and too worldly, to take the freedoms he helped unleash too far from the marketplace. In 1960s Europe, a different story emerged, as African American free jazz innovations by Ornette Coleman, John Coltrane, Albert Ayler and others flowed into cultural traditions from Scandinavia to Spain, Soviet Russia and East Germany, inviting unions with contemporary classical and local folk music along the way.But Miles’s unique sound remained as a key inspiration to two gifted trumpeters in Poland’s Tomasz Stańko (1942-2018) and the Italian Enrico Rava, even as they also drew on European eclecticism. Rava continues to rip through the walls of linear post-bop mazes, and use raw sound as if it were his everyday speech, just as Miles once did – as confirmed by Corners, recorded with his young Fearless Five group plus his longtime friend Joe Lovano on saxophones. Continue reading...

primary_source.headline: Spice Girls: The Singles Collection review – stop fleecing your fans right now, thank you very much
primary_source.content: (Virgin)The reunion that fans were hoping for turns out to be a cash-grab box set – though there is a worthwhile curio featuring Posh on lead vocalsIs there a more taunted fanbase than that of the Spice Girls? Seemingly every other week a story – usually perpetuated by Mel B, the band’s number one cheerleader – appears in the tabloids hinting at some sort of reunion. Or film. Or documentary. Swift denials then emerge, typically linked to Geri or Victoria, and all is calm until a week or so later.So when teasers showing landmarks from 1996’s Wannabe video suddenly appeared on the band’s official social media accounts in September, it felt as if the fans had something tangible to celebrate. The comments quickly filled with hopes of another reunion tour following 2007’s full-band jaunt and 2019’s Posh-less stadium trek. In a music landscape littered with nostalgia tours, surely Ginger, Scary, Baby, Sporty and (maybe) Posh could strap on some Buffalo boots for a final zig-a-zig-ah? Continue reading...

stories.primary_headline: Post your questions for folk music legend Judy Collins

primary_source.headline: Post your questions for folk music legend Judy Collins
primary_source.content: Ahead of her farewell UK concert next year, the 87-year-old singer-songwriter will join us to answer your questionsShe has lived an extraordinary life at the forefront of US folk music, but at the age of 87, Judy Collins is getting ready to retire from touring. Her farewell UK concert at the London Palladium is approaching, and ahead of that she’ll join us to answer your questions.Born in Seattle in 1939, Collins’ career started out in the fertile folk scene of early 1960s New York, and became a close peer of the era’s great singer-songwriters. She recorded Joni Mitchell’s Both Sides, Now, even before Joni Mitchell did – reaching the US Top 10 with her version, which also won a Grammy – and also recorded early versions of songs by Leonard Cohen, Randy Newman and more. A relationship (and its end) with Stephen Stills of Crosby, Stills, Nash and Young resulted in a torrid back-and-forth of poignant songwriting. Continue reading...
